t.2.26.1: Having heard these words of Rāma, the grieving Sītā, her face streaming with tears, softly spoke these words.
t.2.26.2: The hardships you have described concerning life in the forest, know them to be virtues indeed, for my love for you sets them before me as such.
t.2.26.3: By the command of my elders I must go with you; parted from you, Rāma, I would have to give up my life here.
t.2.26.4: O Rāghava, not even Śakra, lord of the gods, could overpower me by his might while I stand by your side.
t.2.26.5: A woman who is bereft of her husband will not be able to live. Indeed, Rāma, such a thing has been shown to me by you.
t.2.26.6: And moreover, O greatly wise one, long ago in my father's house I heard from the brāhmaṇas that it is truly my lot to dwell in the forest.
t.2.26.7: Having heard, while still in my father's house, the word of brahmins skilled in reading auspicious marks, I have always been eager to dwell in the forest, O mighty one.
t.2.26.8: The command to dwell in the forest must indeed be received by me as well. So I will go there with you, beloved, and not otherwise.
t.2.26.9: I shall see the prophecy made about me fulfilled, for I shall go with you. The time for it has now come; let the brahmin prove true to his word.
t.2.26.10: For I know, O hero, that in dwelling in the forest sorrows of many kinds are indeed surely met with by men whose selves are undisciplined.
t.2.26.11: And when I was still a maiden in my father's house, I heard that I would dwell in the forest, foretold by a mendicant woman of virtuous conduct, there in the presence of my mother.
t.2.26.12: Indeed, my lord, you were already entreated in many ways before, for going to dwell in the forest together with you has long been my desire.
t.2.26.13: Bless you, Rāghava, I am resolved upon going, for the way of life of forest-dwelling, the life of a hero, truly pleases me.
t.2.26.14: O pure-souled one, through the power of my love I shall become free from sin as I follow my husband, for my husband is my deity.
t.2.26.15: Even in the state after death, my union with you will be auspicious; for a sacred tradition of the illustrious brahmins is heard to this effect.
t.2.26.16: O wise one, the woman who in this world is given by her fathers to a man with water, according to their own dharma, remains his even in the state after death.
t.2.26.17: Thus, for what reason here do you not consent to take me away from this place, your own wife, virtuous and devoted to her husband?
t.2.26.18: O Kākutstha, you should take me with you, devoted, faithful to my husband, and stricken with grief, me who am the same in joy and sorrow, sharing equally in your happiness and your suffering.
t.2.26.19: If you do not wish to take me, distressed as I am, to the forest, I shall resort to poison, fire, or water for the sake of my death.
t.2.26.20: Thus in many ways she entreated him regarding going with him, but the mighty-armed one did not consent to take her to the desolate forest.
t.2.26.21: Thus addressed, Maithilī fell into anxious thought, as if bathing the earth with the hot tears that fell from her eyes.
t.2.26.22: But the self-possessed Kākutstha, seeking to turn her back from her purpose, consoled Vaidehī at length as she brooded thus, overcome with anger.
